note: Re-attach orphan magic-square nodes to live missions by creating a milestone that links the theorem_id (captain doc: linking grants mission membership, permanently). Titles follow the source-index convention where the source has one.

entries.title: MacMahon (1915) - the 3 does not divide t case of the order-three count
entries.milestone_description: For $t$ not divisible by $3$ there is no $3\times3$ magic square of line sum $t$: $M_3(t) = 0$ whenever $3 \nmid t$. Equivalently, $M_3(t)$ is supported on the multiples of three, where MacMahon's formula $M_3(3e) = 2e^2+2e+1$ applies. This is the vanishing half of the goal `magic_count_three_divisible`.

entries.title: BCCG (2003) section 2 - the order-two magic count
entries.milestone_description: Order-two magic squares of line sum $t$: $M_2(t) = 1$ when $2 \mid t$ and $0$ otherwise, the single square being the constant array with every entry $t/2$. A $2\times2$ semi-magic square of line sum $t$ reads $\begin{pmatrix} a & t-a \\ t-a & a\end{pmatrix}$, whose two diagonals are $2a$ and $2(t-a)$; both equal $t$ only when $2a = t$.

entries.title: BCCG (2003) section 2 - the order-two pandiagonal count
entries.milestone_description: With $P_n(t)$ the number of pandiagonal squares in the one-direction reading (semi-magic plus the wrapped diagonals parallel to the main diagonal), $P_2(t) = 1$ when $2 \mid t$ and $0$ otherwise. At order two the two wrapped diagonals are exactly the two main diagonals, so the pandiagonal condition coincides with the magic one.

entries.title: BCCG (2003) - the order-three pandiagonal count P_3
entries.milestone_description: In Beck-Cohen-Cuomo-Gribelyuk's one-direction reading of *pandiagonal* (the wrapped diagonals parallel to the main diagonal; the ascending family is not required), $P_3(t) = \binom{t+2}{2}$, a degree-two polynomial that never vanishes. Every pandiagonal $3\times3$ square of line sum $t$ has the form $M_{ij} = g(i+j)$ for a single $g$ on $\mathbb{Z}/3$, each wrapped diagonal being a cyclic rotation of $(g(0),g(1),g(2))$; the line sum is $g(0)+g(1)+g(2)$.

entries.title: Order three - the two-direction panmagic count
entries.milestone_description: For the stronger predicate requiring *both* broken-diagonal families (descending and ascending) to sum to the line sum, the only square of line sum $t$ is the constant array, so the count is $1$ when $3 \mid t$ and $0$ otherwise. This is the contrast case to the one-direction $P_3$ above: the two readings of *pandiagonal* differ at order three and must never be substituted for one another.

entries.title: General n - every panmagic square is magic
entries.milestone_description: For every order $n > 0$, the panmagic predicate implies the magic one: semi-magicity together with all broken diagonals in both directions entails the two main diagonals, which are the offset-$0$ members of the two families.

entries.title: Normal squares, general n - the magic constant
entries.milestone_description: If an $n\times n$ array has entries exactly $1,2,\dots,n^2$, each used once, and is magic with line sum $s$, then $2s = n\,(n^2+1)$; that is, $s = n(n^2+1)/2$. This is the general-$n$ statement whose $n=3$ instance gives the constant $15$.

entries.title: Semi-magic squares, general n - total sum is n times the line sum
entries.milestone_description: For an $n\times n$ array over an additive commutative monoid in which every row (and hence every column) sums to $S$, the sum of all $n^2$ entries is $n \bullet S$. This aggregation step is what turns a line sum into a total sum in every magic-constant argument.

entries.title: Symmetries, general n - transposition
entries.milestone_description: Transposition preserves the magic condition and the line sum: it permutes the lines, sending rows of $A$ to columns of $A^{\mathsf T}$ and back, and swaps the two main diagonals.

entries.title: Symmetries, general n - horizontal reflection
entries.milestone_description: Reversing the order of the columns, $(i,j) \mapsto (i, n-1-j)$, preserves the magic condition with the same line sum; it permutes the lines and interchanges the two main diagonals.

entries.title: Symmetries, general n - vertical reflection
entries.milestone_description: Reversing the order of the rows, $(i,j) \mapsto (n-1-i, j)$, preserves the magic condition with the same line sum.

entries.title: Symmetries, general n - affine substitution
entries.milestone_description: If $A$ is magic of line sum $S$ and $a,b$ are scalars, the array $A'_{ij} = a\,A_{ij} + b$ is again magic, with line sum $aS + nb$: each line has exactly $n$ entries, so its sum is scaled by $a$ and shifted by $nb$.

entries.title: BCCG (2003) section 2 - the order-two semi-magic count
entries.milestone_description: $H_2(t) = t+1$: a $2\times2$ semi-magic square of line sum $t$ is $\begin{pmatrix} a & t-a \\ t-a & a\end{pmatrix}$ with $0 \le a \le t$, so it is determined by its top-left corner, which ranges over $t+1$ values. This is the $n=2$ instance of the structural statement that $H_n(t)$ is a polynomial of degree $(n-1)^2$.

entries.title: Order two - there is no normal magic square
entries.milestone_description: No $2\times2$ array can have the four distinct entries $1,2,3,4$ and be magic: comparing the first row $a+b=s$ with the main diagonal $a+d=s$ forces $b=d$. The first order at which normal magic squares exist is three.

entries.title: Order three - the magic constant of a normal square is 15
entries.milestone_description: Every normal $3\times3$ magic square has line sum $15$: the entries are exactly $1,\dots,9$, so $s = (1+\cdots+9)/3 = 45/3 = 15$. This is the $n=3$ instance of `magic_constant_of_normal`.

entries.title: Order three - the centre of a normal square is 5
entries.milestone_description: The centre cell of every normal $3\times3$ magic square is $5$. In any order-three magic square of line sum $s$ the centre is $s/3$: adding the middle row, the middle column and the two diagonals counts the centre four times and every other cell once, so $\text{total} + 3\,M_{1,1} = 4s$; with $s = 15$ this gives $M_{1,1} = 5$.

entries.title: Order three - normal squares are associative with complement 10
entries.milestone_description: Every normal $3\times3$ magic square is associative (regular, symmetric through the centre) with complement constant $10$: any two centrally opposite cells satisfy $M_{ij} + M_{2-i,\,2-j} = 10$ for all $0 \le i,j \le 2$. The centre is $5$, and the eight remaining entries split into four opposite pairs summing to $10$.
